source.title: Max-Margin Works while Large Margin Fails: Generalization without Uniform Convergence
source.authors: Margalit R. Glasgow; Colin Wei; Mary K. Wootters; Tengyu Ma

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper proves generalization and non-generalization results for near-max-margin classifiers in theoretical linear and two-layer-network settings, using theoretical bounds rather than the empirical interventions in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study's own theoretical bounds and constructions bear on V1's coexistence of memorization and generalization and on V7's relation between margin and generalization. It does not report empirical tests of architecture comparisons, optimizer choice, batch size, dropout, width sweeps, or removing memorized examples. The results are theorem statements and proof analyses, not measured network runs.
record.test_reason: The study proves generalization bounds for near-max-margin classifiers on clean synthetic distributions. It does not test V1's coexistence of random-label fitting capacity and natural-label generalization under the same training recipe. Its normalized-margin results also do not test V7's magnitude-aware sharpness measure or its ranking of generalization gaps. No other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors prove generalization for near-max-margin solutions in synthetic linear and nonlinear settings, including regimes where uniform convergence fails. Their analysis combines generalizable signal components with data-memorizing components. Guarantees depend on the parameter regime and sufficiently small noise; below the XOR threshold, near-max-margin solutions with chance error exist. Large but non-near-maximal margins can also fail. They leave guarantees for nonlinear gradient-descent solutions that are not near-max-margin open.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proves theoretical bounds and impossibility results in synthetic linear classification and a two-layer network with quadratic XOR ground truth. It does not reproduce the claim's empirical random-label experiments or optimizer, batch-size, regularization, width, sharpness-measure, or example-removal studies.
record.method_sensitivity: Signal-to-noise parameter κ and activation exponent h determine the thresholds. In the XOR problem, below κ_gen near-max-margin solutions may have chance test error; above it the stated generalization theorem applies. The paper also distinguishes near-maximal margin from a constant fraction of maximum margin.

fits_no_version.finding: Near-max-margin linear classifiers and two-layer XOR networks have small population-error bounds in specified parameter regimes, with sufficiently small noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near-maximal normalized training margin can guarantee generalization on particular overparameterized synthetic classification problems.

fits_no_version.finding: Below the XOR generalization threshold, a near-max-margin classifier with population error exactly 1/2 exists with high probability.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near-maximal margin need not guarantee generalization below a distribution-dependent threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Generalizing near-max-margin solutions can contain data-memorizing components, while useful one-sided uniform-convergence bounds and polynomial margin bounds fail under the paper's assumptions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization can coexist with memorizing components even where specified classical generalization bounds cannot explain it.

record.problems: Evidence is theoretical and limited to stylized synthetic distributions and assumed near-max-margin solutions. The text notes that it is not guaranteed gradient descent finds a max-margin solution in the non-convex setting; it leaves generalization for non-max-margin neural-network solutions as an open direction.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported empirical findings on the claim were found. The paper's stated theorem bounds and constructions are represented in the rows above; related-work results are not included as this study's own results.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and held-out chance performance compared with natural-label generalization using the same architectures and training recipes.
Test-error changes from widening networks beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout interventions and their dependence on data size, configuration, and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples compared with equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: Theoretical evidence is eligible in principle, but these results address different claims from V1–V8. Memorizing junk features on clean data is not the random-label capacity comparison in V1, and normalized margin is not the sharpness measure in V7. The record's verdicts should therefore be removed.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test random-label fitting or natural-label training recipes on CIFAR-10 or ImageNet, nor the cited Inception, AlexNet, MLP, or Zhang et al. settings. It considers clean synthetic distributions and near-max-margin solutions.
The paper does not sweep network width beyond interpolation.
The paper does not compare convolutional and fully connected architectures.
The paper does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD.
The paper does not vary batch size or training duration.
The paper does not test dropout.

Does not measure magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or compare it against norm- and margin-based measures. It proves results about normalized training margin and generalization for theoretical synthetic settings.
The paper does not identify and remove influential memorized examples.

rows.subject: linear classifier w ∈ R^d
rows.operation_detail: Theorem bounds test loss for any near-max-margin classifier under the linear synthetic data distribution.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n) over training set
rows.note: The result applies to any classifier meeting the near-max-margin condition; it is a theorem, not a measured run.
rows.check: Theorem 3.1 bounds population error on clean synthetic data; it provides no paired random-label and natural-label training result for V1. The training-sample condition is d/n ≥ c, not nd ≥ c. This is a theoretical guarantee, not a measured run.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network f_W
rows.size_stated: m hidden units; dimension d ≥ cn
rows.operation_detail: Theorem bounds test loss for any near-max-margin network under the quadratic XOR synthetic data distribution.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n/c) over training set
rows.note: Synthetic quadratic ground truth; theorem covers all networks meeting the stated margin condition.
rows.check: Theorem 3.3 concerns clean synthetic XOR labels and assumed near-max-margin solutions, not V1's random-label capacity comparison. The condition is d/n ≥ c, not nd ≥ c. The error bound becomes small when σ is sufficiently small; crossing the κ threshold alone does not ensure near-zero error.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network f_W
rows.size_stated: m hidden units; dimension d ≥ cn
rows.operation_detail: Constructs a near-max-margin classifier with zero signal-space component in the XOR setting.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n/c) over training set that such a classifier exists
rows.note: Shows that near-maximal margin alone need not ensure generalization below the threshold; it is an existence result.
rows.check: The chance-error construction concerns near-max-margin solutions on clean XOR data below a threshold. It neither tests nor limits V1's paired random-label and natural-label finding. It establishes existence of a bad solution, not failure of every solution or of a training algorithm.

rows.subject: linear classifier w ∈ R^d
rows.operation_detail: Relates near-maximal normalized training margin to test loss in the linear problem.
rows.measure: 0/1 test loss as a function of training margin and signal-to-noise parameters
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n) over training set
rows.note: This supports a relationship involving extremal training margin, but does not measure perturbation sharpness or rank competing empirical measures.
rows.check: Normalized training margin is not magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness. This duplicates R1's theorem and cannot establish V7's correlation or comparative ranking. Theorem 3.1 requires δ ≤ κ ≤ 1/δ; Theorem C.4 permits any κ > 0 with κ-dependent dimension and margin-tolerance conditions. The condition nd ≥ c is incorrect.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network f_W
rows.size_stated: m hidden units; dimension d ≥ cn
rows.operation_detail: Relates near-maximal normalized training margin to test loss in the quadratic XOR problem.
rows.measure: 0/1 test loss as a function of extremal normalized training margin
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n/c) over training set
rows.note: The theorem concerns normalized margin, not magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness.
rows.check: This duplicates R2's theorem under a different interpretation. It bounds test error using near-maximal normalized margin and does not measure sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, or competing empirical measures.

rows.subject: two-layer neural network f_W
rows.size_stated: m hidden units; dimension d ≥ cn
rows.operation_detail: Establishes a region where a near-max-margin classifier can have chance test error.
rows.uncertainty: Probability at least 1−3e^(−n/c) over training set that such a classifier exists
rows.note: Limits any broad claim that large or maximal margin alone tracks a small generalization gap; the theorem is an existence statement below the generalization threshold.
rows.check: This duplicates R3's existence result. Chance error for a near-max-margin solution is not a reversal of V7: no magnitude-aware sharpness is evaluated, and no sharpness–gap association is established.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Linear and quadratic synthetic distributions above the stated signal-to-noise thresholds, for near-max-margin classifiers
reader_labels.reason: Test loss is bounded near zero for qualifying classifiers (R1, R2), while the paper's analysis describes simultaneous signal and data-memorizing components.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Quadratic XOR synthetic distribution below κ_gen^{XOR,h}
reader_labels.reason: A near-max-margin classifier with chance test error exists in this regime (R3); this qualifies the generalization result by threshold and solution choice.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Near-max-margin classifiers on the stated synthetic distributions
reader_labels.reason: The theorems connect extremal training margin with generalization in specified regimes but do not test magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness or its comparative ranking (R4, R5); below threshold the relationship can fail (R6).
